Even though Genghis Khan was dead and the political situation in the empire was volatile, the Mongol conquests continued. A big army under Batu and Subutai invaded Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Hungary, Serbia, and Bulgaria. Meanwhile, the resurgence of the Khwarezmian empire under Jalal ad-din drew the Mongols back to Iran. This sparked a conflict with the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum that culminated in the battle of Kose Dag (Kösedağ) in 1243. Under Hulagu, the Mongols attacked the Abbasids and sacked Baghdad in 1258, but with the succession crisis looming he returned to Mongolia. His general Kitbuqa was left in the area with a smaller force and fought the battle of Ain Jalut against the forces of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars in 1260. This battle would become the high point of the Mongol invasions in the West.

In 1258, the Mongol Empire, led by Hulagu Khan, laid siege to Baghdad, the thriving capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and the heart of the Islamic Golden Age. In this video, we uncover how the Mongols conquered Baghdad, why the Abbasids were unable to defend their empire, and how this moment marked the end of the Islamic Golden Age. From political intrigue and military strategy to the cultural aftermath, this is the story of the fall of Baghdad — a tragedy that reshaped the Middle East forever.

snippet.title: The Mongol Sack of Baghdad 1258
snippet.description:
The Siege of Baghdad in 1258 was a turning point in world history. The city, the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and the jewel of the Islamic world, was sacked by a massive Mongol army under Hulagu Khan.

This wasn't just a conquest—it was an annihilation. The Mongols, numbering over 138,000 men, breached the city's walls on February 10th and spent a full week pillaging, burning, and slaughtering. Estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to as high as 2 million.

Key topics explored in this video:

The Rise of Hulagu Khan: The Mongol prince sent west to secure Persia and his ultimate target: Baghdad.

The Caliph's Downfall: The arrogance of Caliph al-Musta'sim and his failure to provide reinforcements, which convinced Hulagu to overthrow him.

The Siege Itself: The Mongol use of Chinese artillery, the breaching of the walls, and the swift, 13‑day collapse of the city's defenses.

The Aftermath: The systematic destruction of mosques, hospitals, libraries, and palaces.

The Legacy: How this event is traditionally seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age, though modern historians debate its true impact.

This is the story of the end of a world. Click play to learn more.

snippet.title: What the Mongols Did to Baghdad’s Royal Family Was a Warning to the World
snippet.description:
What the Mongols Did to Baghdad's Royal Family Was a Warning to the World
They didn't kill him quickly.
They made him walk through his own treasury first.
February 1258. The Caliph of Baghdad, spiritual heir to Muhammad, ruler of the Islamic world's greatest city - was forced to witness the gold he'd hoarded while his walls crumbled. Three hours later, he was dead. But not by blade. Not by arrow. The method the Mongols chose was designed to send a message that would echo across continents.
What happened next wasn't just execution. It was communication written in blood.
The Caliph was wrapped in a carpet and crushed under horses no blood touching the ground, respecting Mongol taboo while violating every assumption about power and protection. His sons were eliminated. His daughters vanished into Mongol camps. His lineage 37 generations tracing back to the Prophet was severed in a single day.
But the royal family's fate was just the beginning.
Baghdad burned for 13 days. The House of Wisdom centuries of accumulated knowledge went up in flames. The Tigris River ran black with ink from thrown manuscripts. Between 90,000 and 1,000,000 died. The center of Islamic civilization was erased not in rage, but as a calculated demonstration.

Within weeks, every ruler from Damascus to Delhi knew exactly what defiance cost. Cities surrendered without seeing a single Mongol soldier. Kings sent tribute before armies arrived. The warning worked so well, the Mongols never had to repeat it.
From Hulagu Khan's systematic siege doctrine to the carpet execution that became legend, this is the story of how one royal family's destruction reshaped an entire civilization's approach to power.\

snippet.title: How the Mongols Conquered Baghdad (And Trampled Its Ruler)
snippet.description:
In February 1258, the Mongol army of Hulegu Khan arrived at Baghdad — the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, home to one million people, and the intellectual center of the medieval world. The Caliph al-Musta'sim believed the city's spiritual prestige would deter attack. He didn't prepare an army. He didn't reinforce the walls.
Hulegu arrived with the largest force the Mongols had ever assembled. His artillery was commanded by a Han Chinese general. His engineers broke the city's dike system and flooded the ground behind the Caliph's army, trapping them. The walls fell in two weeks.
The Caliph was captured and forced to watch as his citizens were massacred and his treasury looted. Hulegu then locked him in his own treasure room — surrounded by the gold he had refused to spend on his city's defense.
Then came the execution. Mongol law forbade royal blood from touching the earth. So they rolled the last Caliph of Baghdad in a carpet and rode their horses over him until he was dead.
The Tigris ran black from the ink of books thrown into the river and red from the blood of the scholars who wrote them. The Islamic Golden Age ended in thirteen days. Baghdad never recovered its former status.

snippet.title: 1258: The Mongol Siege That Shattered Baghdad
snippet.description:
Discover the full story of the Mongol Siege of Baghdad in 1258. In this documentary, we explore how Hulagu Khan and the Mongol Empire brought an end to the Islamic Golden Age and the Abbasid Caliphate.

Baghdad believed history would protect it — but history could not stop the Mongol war machine.

In 1258, the city of the Abbasid caliphs faced one of the most devastating disasters of the medieval world: the Mongol siege and sack of Baghdad. For nearly five hundred years, Baghdad had been more than a capital. It was a symbol of scholarship, sacred legitimacy, imperial memory, libraries, courts, poets, merchants, and political authority. But by the thirteenth century, the power behind that symbol had weakened.

This episode of The History Docket reopens the fall of Baghdad as a case file. We examine the final Abbasid caliph, al-Musta’sim, the advance of Hulegu Khan, the terrifying logic of Mongol conquest, the failed diplomacy, the divided court, the accusations against Ibn al-Alqami, and the fatal gap between prestige and military reality.

Was Baghdad destroyed only by Mongol brutality? Or was the disaster made possible by Abbasid miscalculation, political fragmentation, weak preparation, and the dangerous belief that a famous name could defend a city?

The fall of Baghdad did not erase Islamic civilization, and the story is more complex than the famous images of rivers of ink and ruined libraries. But 1258 shattered the Abbasid caliphate in its historic capital and changed the political map of the region.

If this investigation grips you, like the episode, subscribe to The History Docket, and leave your verdict in the comments: who carries the greatest responsibility for the fall of Baghdad — Hulegu, al-Musta’sim, the Abbasid court, or the divided world around them?

snippet.title: Baghdad Burns: Fall of the Abbasids
snippet.description:
In the 8th century Middle East, a new dynasty seized control of one of the world’s greatest empires – the Islamic Caliphate. Though little remembered in the west today, the Abbasids reigned for five centuries. They oversaw an era of Islamic military dominance... city-building… brilliant scholarship, and technological innovation. It has come to be remembered as Islam’s ‘golden age’. This is the story of the Abbasid Caliphate.

In the 8th century Middle East, a new dynasty seized control of one of the world’s greatest empires – the Islamic Caliphate. snippet.title: Mongols at Baghdad’s Gates: The Brutal 1258 Siege That Turned the Tigris Black and Ended an Empire
snippet.description:
150,000 Mongols under Hulegu Khan smashed Baghdad in 1258 and ended the Abbasid Caliphate in a single week. This video breaks down the Siege of Baghdad step by step: the ignored ultimatum, Mongol siege tactics (trebuchets, fire arrows, sappers), the breach on 10 February, the massacre of defenders and civilians, the destruction of the House of Wisdom, and the execution of Caliph Al-Musta'sim. See how the fall of Baghdad shattered the Islamic Golden Age and changed medieval history forever.

What cracked first—walls or will? Which tactic actually broke the city—engines, sappers, or starvation? Drop your take in the comments.

What you’ll learn:

Why Hulegu Khan targeted Baghdad and how his army was built

How Mongol engineering and logistics overwhelmed the city’s defenses

The real death toll estimates (200,000–800,000) and why sources differ

How the Tigris River “turned black with ink” after the House of Wisdom burned

The political and cultural aftermath across the Muslim world and Europe


Comment the single change you’d make to save Baghdad. Walls, allies, or strategy—choose one !

snippet.title: Siege of Baghdad 1258: Mongol Destruction
snippet.description:
In 1258, Baghdad was the center of the world. In seven days, it was erased.

The Siege of Baghdad (1258) was not just another medieval battle — it was one of the most devastating events in human history. When Hulagu Khan and the Mongol Empire reached the gates of the Abbasid capital, they didn’t simply conquer a city. They shattered the heart of the Islamic Golden Age.

The House of Wisdom.
Centuries of scientific advancement.
Astronomy, medicine, mathematics, philosophy.
All gone in days.

This video explores how the Mongol invasion destroyed Baghdad, what really happened during the sack of the city, and how the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate changed the course of world history. From the destruction of irrigation systems to the loss of irreplaceable manuscripts, the consequences of 1258 echoed for centuries.

We break down:
• Why Baghdad fell
• Hulagu Khan’s strategy
• The destruction of the House of Wisdom
• The impact on the Islamic Golden Age
• How the Mongols were finally stopped at the Battle of Ain Jalut

One city.
Seven days.
An incalculable loss.

If you’re interested in medieval history, the Mongol Empire, or the rise and fall of civilizations, this is the story you need to understand.
